npnormalize

npnormalize turns nonprofit names and addresses into keys that can be matched. It is the normalizer shared by three packages:

  • npmatch normalizes each record it matches;
  • matchdb stores the same keys for every organization it holds;
  • pfmatch normalizes grant recipients before matching them.

A record and the reference it is matched against must be normalized by the same code. Otherwise matches quietly stop being found, with no error. This package holds that code in one place, and fingerprints it.

Install 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("Nonprofit-Open-Data-Collective/npnormalize")

Use 

library(npnormalize)

d <- data.frame(name   = c("The Children's Museum of NH", "St. Luke's Hospital Fdn, Inc."),
                dba    = "",
                street = c("6 Washington Pl Ste 300", "PO Box 1558"),
                unit   = NA,
                zip5   = c("03820", "75201-1234"),
                zip_plus4 = NA,
                state  = c("NH", "Texas"))
np_normalize(d)[, c("name_key", "name_core", "street_key", "street_unit_id", "zip5", "state_abb")]
#>                 name_key                       name_core      street_key street_unit_id  zip5 state_abb
#> 1 CHILDRENS MUSEUM OF NH             CHILDRENS MUSEUM NH 6 WASHINGTON PL            300 03820        NH
#> 2   SAINT LUKES HOSPITAL SAINT LUKES HOSPITAL FOUNDATION     PO BOX 1558           <NA> 75201        TX

Input columns. The frame needs the columns name, dba, street, unit, zip5, zip_plus4 and state, with NA or "" where a value is unknown. These are npmatch’s canonical fields, which npmatch::np_query() and npmatch::np_reference() produce from any dataset. division is used when present.

Columns added: * name keys: name_key, name_full, name_core, dba_key; * name features: name_form, name_nums, name_ord, name_placeholder; * street parts: street_key, street_num, street_name, street_type, street_unit, street_unit_id, is_po_box; * ZIP parts: zip5, zip3, zip9; * state_abb.

np_name_core() and np_name_placeholder() work on bare name strings.

Statistics over the keys: * np_name_freq() counts how many records share each name key. * np_token_idf() weights each name token by how rare it is. * np_addr_freq() counts the records at each address and suite, and classifies the address as federated, shared, building or cluster.

The signature 

np_normalize_signature()
#> [1] "v1-3e7b9f9d59bbb19e"

The signature is a hash of the rule tables and functions behind the keys and statistics, so it changes when their behaviour changes. * What it ignores: comments and formatting. * What it leaves out: the matching code in npmatch (comparison, scoring, vetoes), because nothing it computes is stored.

Anything that stores keys should stamp the signature when it is built, and refuse to load under a different one. matchdb does this for its database, bundles and tranches. np_normalize_signature(detail = TRUE) shows which rule table or function moved.

The code was moved here from npmatch unchanged, so the signature is the one npmatch reported (dev/EXTRACTION.md). A test pins the value. Changing the normalizer is allowed, but it is a deliberate release: update the pin and rebuild what depends on it.
